translations.text: The man used to go up from his city, Ramathaim, day after day to worship and offer sacrifices [?] to the Lord God of hosts at Shiloh. Eli the priest was there with his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, who served as priests of the Lord.
She rose after they had eaten at Shiloh and stood before the Lord. Eli the priest was sitting on the [?] at the gates of the Lord’s temple.
She said to him, “Your servant has found favor in your eyes.” The woman went on her way, entered her lodging, sat down, and ate with her husband. She drank, and her face was no longer sad.
She drank. And when the time came, she gave birth to a son and named him Samuel, saying, “I asked the Lord of hosts for him.”
“It was for this little child that I prayed to him, and the Lord granted me the request I made of him.”
The Lord is the one who kills, and he is also the one who gives life. He brings people down to the realm of the dead and brings them up.
He grants the vow of the one who makes a vow and blesses the years of the righteous, for a mighty man’s strength is not his own.

Therefore, this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: “I said that your household and your father’s household would walk before me, serving me forever. But now,” says the Lord, “this will not happen. Those who honor me I will honor, but whoever dishonors me I will dishonor.”
Samuel did not yet know God, and the word of the Lord had not been revealed to him.
The Lord said to Samuel, “Look, I will carry out my words in Israel, so that the ears of everyone who hears them will ring.”

They sent for and gathered all the rulers of the Philistines and said to them, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel. Let it return to its own place so that it does not kill us and the rest of our people.” For a great and very severe affliction had come upon the whole city when the ark of the God of Israel was there.
The Israelites removed the Baals and the groves of Ashtoreth and served the Lord alone.
His resting place was Ramathaim, because his house was there. He judged Israel there, and there he built an altar to the Lord.
“Just as in everything they have done to me from the day I brought them out of the land of Egypt until today, abandoning me and serving other gods, so they are treating you too.”
“He will take your male servants and your female servants, your good cattle and your sheep, and put them to work for him.”
Samuel said to all the people of Israel, “Look, I have listened to your voice in everything you said to me, and I have appointed a king over you.”
All the people said to Samuel, “Pray to the Lord your God for your servants, so that we do not die. For we have added to all our sins and our wickedness by asking for a king over us.”
Samuel said to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil, but do not turn aside and withdraw from the Lord. Instead, serve the Lord with all your heart.”
“For the Lord will not abandon his people, because of his great name. For, as the Lord has done, he has taken you to himself as his people because of his great name.”
“But if you and your kings sin wickedly, the Lord will bring your enemies against you.”
Jonathan came out from among the Philistines at the edge of Michmash. He did not tell his father.
One of the roads led northward up to Michmash, and the other led from the south up to Gibeah.
Samuel did everything the Lord had told him and went up to Bethlehem. The elders of the city were astonished when they saw him, and they said to him, “Is your coming peaceful, seer?”
David was the son of an Ephrathite man from Bethlehem in Judah named Jesse, who had eight sons. In Saul’s days, this man was old and advanced in years.
The Philistine came forward against them every day, morning and evening, for forty days.
I would go after it and strike the lion, so that what the lion had seized came out of its mouth. If it turned against me, I would seize it by its beard, overpower it, and kill it.
The Philistine also advanced toward David, boasting, with his shield-bearer ahead of him.
The Philistine said to David, “Am I like a dog that you come out against with a club and stones?” David said to him, “Perhaps you are worse than a dog.” And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.

The men of Israel and the men of Judah rose up, shouted, and pursued the Philistines as far as the road leading into Gath, advancing into it, and as far as the gates of Ashkelon. The slain Philistines fell along the road of the gates, as far as Gath and Ekron.
David acted wisely in all his ways, and the Lord was with him.
When Saul saw that David acted very wisely, he became afraid of him.
Saul instructed his servants, saying to them, “Speak privately with David and tell him, ‘Look, the king wants you, and all his other servants love you. So agree to marry the king’s daughter.’”
If your father makes inquiries about me, tell him, “He earnestly asked me to let him go to Bethlehem, his town, because a sacrifice for the whole clan will take place there at the appointed time.”
And while I am still alive, you will show me mercy, but also in death, if I die.

Saul became very angry with Jonathan and said to him, “You son of women who have been cast out! Don’t I know that you are a friend of Jesse’s son, to your own shame and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?”
Jonathan answered his father, saying, “Why should he die? What sin has he committed?”
One of Saul’s servants was there that day, detained there without freedom in his master’s presence. His name was Doeg the Edomite, and he tended Saul’s mules.

He changed his behavior before him and kept beating his hands against the doors of the city gate. That day he acted like those who are out of their minds. He limped this way and that before them, falling down at the doors of the gate, with his saliva running over his beard.
“Am I short of madmen, that you have brought this man to me to behave like this in my presence? This man will not enter my house!”
“Now, you king of Israel, whom are you looking for? What sort of thing are you pursuing? You are pursuing a dead dog and chasing a single flea.”
“May the Lord be judge and arbiter between me and you. May the Lord look, judge my case, and take his seat with you.”
David swore an oath to Saul. Saul went up to his own place, and David and his men went up to Messara, the fortified place.
When morning came, he had sobered up from the wine, and his wife told him these things. When he heard them, his heart sank within him, and he became rigid, like stone.
The Philistines gathered, came, and encamped at Shunem. Saul also gathered with all Israel at Gilboa.
Achish answered David, saying, “I know that you are good in my eyes, but the Philistine leaders say, ‘He must not go out with us to war.’”
David said to him, “Whose man are you, and where are you from?” He said, “I am a young Egyptian, the slave of an Amalekite man. My master abandoned me because I fell ill three days ago.”

He brought me to that place, and there they were, spread out over the whole land, eating and drinking and rejoicing over all the plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.
Those in Beth-zur, those in Ramah in the south, and those in Jattir.
